paragraphs: Causal representation learning tries to recover underlying causal variables from complex observations. This paper considers measurements that reveal only part of the underlying state, with the visible subset changing from one example to another. The observations are also unpaired, so the learner cannot rely on matched views of the same state to connect the missing pieces.

The main contribution is two identifiability results: statements about when the underlying variables can be distinguished from the observations. One covers linear mixing functions without imposing a parametric form on the causal model. The other covers piecewise linear mixing functions when the latent causal variables are Gaussian. These are distinct results with different conditions.

The authors use these insights to develop two estimation methods that encourage sparse inferred representations. Sparsity connects the learning procedure to the setting in which each measurement exposes only a subset of variables. Experiments on simulated data and established benchmarks support the methods’ ability to recover ground-truth latents under the evaluated conditions.
icml-2024-a-sparsity-principle-for-parti.tldr: Sparsity helps recover latent causal variables from unpaired, partially observed data, with identifiability results for two specified mixing settings.

paragraphs: Mutual transfer learning improves predictions by sharing knowledge between related domains. In a federated setting, deciding which participants should learn together becomes an important part of personalization. This paper focuses on recovering that learnability structure, rather than assuming that every participant benefits equally from the same shared information.

The proposed method, AdaGrP, determines its recovery threshold adaptively through a nonparametric procedure called adaptive threshold correction. This addresses the expensive threshold tuning associated with earlier clustered federated approaches. The authors also position the method against centralized transfer approaches that struggle to adapt when the concepts being learned change.

The theoretical analysis guarantees perfect learnability recovery with the corrected threshold under the paper’s relaxed condition. That guarantee should be read within its stated setting. Empirically, AdaGrP improves learnability structure recovery by an average of 16.9% over the compared state-of-the-art clustered federated learning baselines. The reported gain concerns recovering relationships for learning; it is not presented as an equivalent percentage improvement in prediction accuracy.
icml-2024-adaptive-group-personalization.tldr: AdaGrP adaptively selects a grouping threshold to recover federated learnability structure without threshold tuning.

paragraphs: Soft pseudo-labels describe a model’s predictions as probabilities across classes instead of a single definitive label. They can carry information useful for training another predictor. This paper argues that ordinary classification objectives are poorly aligned with generating these labels: selecting the correct class and capturing useful knowledge in a probability distribution are different goals.

Designing a better objective directly is difficult because datasets generally do not provide ground-truth soft labels. The authors instead learn the objective through a meta-network. Their framework alternates between training the predictive model and training the pseudo-label generator, while adjusting the objective using feedback from both models’ performance on the learning task.

This makes the usefulness of the generated labels part of how the generator itself is trained. The framework can also accommodate different learning tasks through changes to the task loss. Benchmark experiments support its effectiveness. The central contribution is therefore a way to learn an aligned training signal when direct supervision for the desired soft labels is unavailable.
icml-2024-aligned-objective-for-soft-pse.tldr: A learned objective trains soft pseudo-label generators using feedback from both the generator and the predictor that consumes its labels.

paragraphs: Tabular data pose structural challenges for deep learning: feature directions have distinct meanings, and useful information can be sparse across features. BiSHop addresses both through an end-to-end architecture designed around the organization of a table. Its motivation comes from the connection between associative memory mechanisms and attention.

The model processes data sequentially in two directions, using interconnected modules for column-wise and row-wise learning. Each module contains generalized sparse modern Hopfield layers, which extend the underlying memory model with learnable sparsity. The architecture learns representations at multiple scales, capturing interactions within features and between features while adapting sparsity at each scale.

This design combines directional processing with selective representation learning instead of treating sparsity as a fixed setting throughout the model. Across diverse real-world datasets, the authors report performance exceeding the compared state-of-the-art methods while requiring significantly fewer hyperparameter optimization runs. Those findings suggest that the architecture can improve both predictive results and the tuning effort needed to obtain them in the evaluated tabular tasks.
icml-2024-bishop-bi-directional-cellular.tldr: BiSHop combines row-wise and column-wise learning with adaptive sparse Hopfield layers to improve tabular prediction and reduce tuning effort.

paragraphs: Forecasting several quantities at once requires uncertainty estimates for their joint outcome. A separate interval for one response does not itself describe the full multivariate result. This paper introduces MultiDimSPCI, a sequential conformal prediction method that constructs ellipsoidal prediction regions for multivariate responses, with particular attention to time series.

Time series create a challenge because their observations are not exchangeable: temporal ordering and dependence matter. The theoretical contribution is a finite-sample, high-probability bound on the conditional coverage gap. This quantifies uncertainty about how closely conditional coverage approaches its target, rather than asserting that conditional coverage is always exactly correct.

Experiments show valid coverage across a wide range of evaluated multivariate time series, alongside smaller prediction regions than the compared conformal and non-conformal baselines. Smaller regions are useful when they retain coverage because they narrow the range of plausible joint outcomes. The contribution combines sequential multivariate uncertainty estimation with theoretical coverage analysis and empirical evidence of more compact regions.
icml-2024-conformal-prediction-for-multi.tldr: MultiDimSPCI builds compact multivariate time-series prediction regions with finite-sample bounds on the conditional coverage gap.

paragraphs: Moderately sized language models can translate well but may lag behind leading translation systems and larger language models. This paper examines whether the training objective contributes to that gap. It identifies quality problems in reference translations, including human-generated references, that limit the value of simply training a model to imitate them.

The authors introduce Contrastive Preference Optimization, or CPO, to steer models away from translations that are acceptable yet fall short of the desired quality. The change shifts training toward translation preferences rather than relying only on reference imitation. Applied to ALMA models, the approach uses 22,000 parallel sentences and updates 0.1% of the parameters.

The resulting ALMA-R model shows substantial improvements and can match or exceed WMT competition winners and GPT-4 on the WMT’21, WMT’22, and WMT’23 test datasets. These findings demonstrate the potential of preference-based training to close translation performance gaps with a comparatively small adaptation. The reported comparisons concern those translation evaluations, rather than general language-model capability.
icml-2024-contrastive-preference-optimiz.tldr: CPO improves ALMA translation models through preference-based training, producing competitive results with limited data and parameter updates.

paragraphs: Vision transformers contain both attention modules and feedforward networks, but architectural improvements often concentrate on attention. This paper studies the feedforward component instead. Its theoretical analysis identifies providing nonlinearity as the component’s primary role and relates the degree of that nonlinearity to the number of hidden dimensions.

The authors use this relationship to design an improved feedforward network, IFFN. It incorporates an arbitrary GeLU function, called AGeLU, and combines multiple instances to increase nonlinearity. A spatial enhancement component adds further nonlinear capacity. The intended tradeoff is to make the nonlinear transformations richer so that the network can use fewer hidden dimensions and require less computation.

Experiments apply the module to a broad range of leading vision transformers with different attention mechanisms and overall architectures. On ImageNet classification, the authors report reductions in operation counts and parameter counts without sacrificing accuracy. The result points to feedforward design as a useful efficiency improvement that can accompany multiple existing approaches to transformer attention.
icml-2024-enhancing-vision-transformer-a.tldr: IFFN strengthens feedforward nonlinearity so vision transformers can use fewer hidden dimensions while preserving evaluated ImageNet accuracy.

paragraphs: Learning three-dimensional dynamics involves understanding both interactions between objects and how those interactions evolve over time. Graph neural networks can model spatial relationships, but the paper argues that next-step prediction does not faithfully capture temporal correlations. EGNO instead treats the evolving trajectory as the object to be learned.

The method represents dynamics as a function of time and uses neural operators to approximate that function. Its temporal convolutions are parameterized in Fourier space and stacked over equivariant networks. This combines explicit temporal modeling with SE(3) equivariance: predictions remain consistent with rotations and translations of the three-dimensional system.

The approach matters because it builds time dependence and spatial symmetry into the same model, rather than relying only on individual next-step predictions to express motion. Experiments cover particle simulations, human motion capture, and molecular dynamics. The authors report significantly better performance than existing methods across these evaluations and attribute the gains to equivariant temporal modeling. The evidence supports trajectory-level modeling across the tested domains.
icml-2024-equivariant-graph-neural-opera.tldr: EGNO learns complete time-dependent 3D trajectories while preserving rotation and translation equivariance.

paragraphs: Sparse phase retrieval asks how to reconstruct a signal when measurements omit phase information and only a small subset of the signal’s entries are nonzero. The paper describes an n-dimensional signal with k nonzero entries. Its focus is the initialization stage that supplies a starting estimate for reconstruction.

For most existing reconstruction algorithms discussed in the abstract, initialization dominates sampling complexity: obtaining a suitable starting point determines much of the measurement requirement. The authors propose exponential spectral pursuit, or ESP, to improve this stage. Targeting initialization matters because a demanding starting procedure can remain a bottleneck even when subsequent reconstruction is effective.

The theoretical result gives ESP a tighter sampling-complexity bound than leading initialization methods such as the truncated power method. Experiments also show better performance than existing initialization approaches for sparse phase retrieval. Together, these findings support ESP as an improved way to begin reconstruction. The contribution concerns the measurement demands and effectiveness of initialization, rather than a separately claimed redesign of every stage of signal recovery.
icml-2024-exponential-spectral-pursuit-a.tldr: ESP improves sparse phase-retrieval initialization through a tighter sampling-complexity bound and stronger empirical performance.

paragraphs: Imitation learning inherits weaknesses from its demonstrations, especially when examples are scarce and imperfect. Online reinforcement learning can refine the resulting policy, often with KL regularization to stabilize updates. This paper finds that imperfect demonstrations can bias that refinement, while regularization can further restrict the exploration needed to improve.

Iterative Regularized Policy Optimization, or IRPO, alternates offline imitation learning with online reinforcement exploration. The policy produced by online learning becomes the demonstrator for subsequent iterations. A demonstration-boosting process improves the examples used for later learning, allowing the source of imitation guidance to evolve along with the policy.

The key idea is to repeatedly refresh the demonstrations instead of leaving the initial examples as a persistent source of bias. Experiments on widely used benchmarks and a new fixed-wing UAV control task show improvements in both demonstration quality and policy performance. These results support the iterative interaction between imitation and exploration as a way to learn more effectively from imperfect starting demonstrations.
icml-2024-iterative-regularized-policy-o.tldr: IRPO alternates imitation and reinforcement learning, using improved online policies to strengthen demonstrations for subsequent iterations.

paragraphs: Language models can produce flexible dialogue, but their preferred actions may reflect biases inherited from training data rather than sound strategy. This paper studies that problem in Werewolf, a social deduction game requiring both communication and decision-making. The aim is to combine language generation with action selection trained for strategic play.

The framework assigns different responsibilities to the language model and the reinforcement learning policy. The language model performs deductive reasoning and generates a diverse set of possible actions. The trained policy then chooses which candidate to use in the game. This gives the decision-making component alternatives beyond the language model’s own preferred response.

Experiments show that the resulting agents overcome the identified action bias and outperform existing language-model agents in Werewolf. In human-agent experiments, they also achieve human-level performance and exhibit strong strategic play. These findings support separating candidate generation from learned strategic selection in this testbed. The human-level result refers to the evaluated game setting, rather than unrestricted human-level reasoning.
icml-2024-language-agents-with-reinforce.tldr: An LLM generates candidate actions while a reinforcement learning policy selects strategically effective moves in Werewolf.

paragraphs: One-bit object detectors can perform well on ordinary-sized objects but lose substantial accuracy on tiny ones. The paper links this difficulty to high-level features that do not sufficiently distinguish foreground objects from their surroundings. DFR-Det targets this representation problem for tiny-object detection in aerial images.

The method uses an information bottleneck to refine features toward a more distinctive representation of tiny objects. A new decoder incorporates a foreground mask to strengthen target-relevant features while suppressing background influence. The decoder can be attached to existing detectors, and the authors state that it adds no extra burden to the inference procedure.

Experiments across several tiny-object detection tasks show better results than state-of-the-art one-bit detectors. One reported example is a DFR-Det version of one-bit FCOS reaching 12.8% average precision on AI-TOD, approaching its real-valued counterpart. The finding suggests that improving foreground discrimination can recover useful detection ability despite severe numerical compression, while retaining the stated inference-cost advantage.
icml-2024-learning-1-bit-tiny-object-det.tldr: DFR-Det improves tiny-object detection in one-bit networks by refining foreground features without adding inference burden.

paragraphs: Subgroup discovery looks for populations whose target properties differ unusually from the broader data. The paper describes applications ranging from demographic analysis to molecular properties. It identifies several obstacles in existing approaches, including requirements to discretize predictive variables beforehand, restrictions on target distributions, scalability problems, and difficulty finding diverse results.

SYFLOW makes subgroup discovery an end-to-end optimization problem centered on maximizing KL divergence. It uses normalizing flows to model arbitrary target distributions, giving the search a way to represent more complex target behavior. A newly introduced neural layer produces interpretable descriptions of the subgroups, connecting the optimization result to understandable population characteristics.

The combination matters because finding an unusual distribution is most useful when the corresponding group can also be described clearly. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world data, together with a case study, show that SYFLOW reliably finds highly exceptional subgroups with insightful descriptions. The stated findings support both the discovery of unusual groups and the interpretability of their descriptions in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-learning-exceptional-subgroups.tldr: SYFLOW jointly learns exceptional subgroups and interpretable descriptions using flexible distribution models and KL-divergence optimization.

paragraphs: A multimodal model must understand information within images and language while also connecting the two. Libra explores an architecture that separates those responsibilities. Its decoupled vision system distinguishes modeling within a modality from interactions across modalities, allowing visual processing to have dedicated structure inside a language-model-based system.

The model adds a routed visual expert and a cross-modal bridge to a pretrained language model. During attention computation, these components route visual and language information so that within-modality processing and cross-modal interaction can use different attention patterns. Training uses discrete autoregressive modeling for both visual and language inputs.

This design matters because the same system can preserve dedicated visual modeling while still supporting comprehension across images and text. Experiments show that Libra forms a strong multimodal language-model baseline, rivaling existing work in image-to-text tasks with 50 million training data. The authors present it as a prototype demonstrating the value of this architectural separation and as a direction for future multimodal foundation models.
icml-2024-libra-building-decoupled-visio.tldr: Libra separates visual processing from cross-modal interaction through a routed visual expert and bridge inside a pretrained language model.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation compresses training information into synthetic data, but image-text learning creates a distinctive challenge. In the setting considered here, examples do not come with an inherent class structure. What matters is the correspondence between modalities: which images and texts should be treated as similar during contrastive learning.

Low-Rank Similarity Mining, or LoRS, distills a ground-truth similarity matrix alongside the image-text pairs themselves. This makes the relationships between examples part of the distilled training setup. Low-rank factorization represents that matrix efficiently, addressing the computational and scaling demands of carrying similarity information together with the synthetic data.

The authors report significant improvements to existing distillation algorithms and recommend LoRS as a foundational synthetic-data setup for image-text distillation. The conceptual contribution is that a compact multimodal dataset can include learned correspondence information as well as the examples. Its stated benefits come from preserving the relational structure needed for image-text learning while using factorization to keep that additional information manageable.
icml-2024-low-rank-similarity-mining-for.tldr: LoRS distills image-text pairs together with a low-rank similarity matrix that preserves cross-modal correspondence efficiently.

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning aims to prepare an agent to learn across tasks, but its generalization can remain tied to the training task distribution. PSBL addresses adaptation when test tasks come from a shifted distribution. It trains a transformer variant to infer a predictive posterior distribution over the optimal policy.

Once meta-training is complete, the network’s parameters remain frozen. The agent updates its approximate posterior through ongoing interaction and samples actions from it to explore. Experience therefore changes the agent’s inferred uncertainty and behavior through context, rather than through additional parameter updates. The abstract describes this process as progressively reducing uncertainty and improving performance.

Experiments compare PSBL with standard meta-reinforcement learning methods under a strictly shifted test-task distribution. The authors report significantly stronger performance in both sparse-reward and dense-reward tasks. These findings support posterior-based in-context adaptation as a way to handle the evaluated distribution shifts. The contribution centers on continuing to learn from interaction after training while keeping the underlying network weights fixed.
icml-2024-meta-reinforcement-learning-ro.tldr: PSBL uses frozen transformer weights to update policy uncertainty in context and explore effectively under tested task-distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection depends partly on the range of features a model represents. Combining models could broaden that range, but only if their representations differ meaningfully. This paper questions whether conventional ensemble diversity, created through different initializations or held-out data, actually delivers the needed variety.

The authors introduce qualitative and quantitative evaluation tools called Loss Basin/Barrier Visualization and Self-Coupling Index. Their analysis finds limited variability in earlier ensembles, including weights related through affine transformations. They propose Multi-Comprehension Ensemble, which creates diversity through distinct supervision tasks. Different tasks encourage different interpretations of the same data and labels, expanding the feature representation field.

Experiments show better out-of-distribution detection than both a naive deep ensemble and a standalone model of comparable size. The contribution is therefore about how to produce useful ensemble diversity, rather than simply increasing the number of models. The reported results support varying supervision as an effective way to broaden representations for the evaluated detection tasks.
icml-2024-out-of-distribution-detection-.tldr: Multi-Comprehension Ensemble improves out-of-distribution detection by training ensemble members on distinct supervision tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies online pricing when purchase decisions depend on both product features and the offered price. Its demand model allows price sensitivity, or elasticity, to vary with those features. The authors show that this can equivalently be expressed through customer valuations whose noise has feature-dependent variability, known as heteroscedasticity.

They develop a computationally efficient algorithm called Pricing with Perturbation. Its regret bound is O(√(dT log T)), where d and T describe contextual dimension and the time horizon. Regret measures the accumulated performance shortfall against the pricing benchmark. The result permits arbitrary adversarial sequences of input contexts, rather than requiring a benign ordering of feature information.

A lower bound of Ω(√(dT)) shows that the upper bound has optimal dependence on d and T up to logarithmic factors. This provides a theoretical benchmark for the algorithm’s efficiency in learning to price. The broader contribution connects two descriptions of demand uncertainty and uses that connection to obtain a pricing method with near-matching performance bounds.
icml-2024-pricing-with-contextual-elasti.tldr: Pricing with Perturbation handles feature-dependent price sensitivity with regret optimal in dimension and horizon up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Preferential Bayesian optimization searches for a good solution when feedback only indicates which of two candidates is preferred. The learner does not receive direct function values. This paper develops a principled way to manage uncertainty and guide that search using pairwise preference information alone.

Inspired by likelihood ratios, the authors construct a confidence set of possible black-box functions. An optimistic algorithm then uses that uncertainty representation to choose promising candidates, supported by an efficient computational method. The analysis gives an information-theoretic bound on cumulative regret and uses it to derive a procedure for reporting an estimated best solution with a guaranteed convergence rate.

Experiments include functions sampled from Gaussian processes, standard test functions, and a thermal comfort optimization problem. The method consistently performs better than or competitively with the compared leading heuristics. Its significance is the combination of practical search performance and theoretical control over accumulated regret and final-solution convergence, guarantees that the compared heuristics do not provide.
icml-2024-principled-preferential-bayesi.tldr: A preference-only Bayesian optimization method combines competitive empirical search with regret and convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Generating audio from text and precisely editing an existing track are different challenges. An editing system must connect a requested change to a target event within the audio. This paper introduces PPAE, a module for diffusion models intended to make that local manipulation more flexible and precise.

The editing instruction comes entirely from a text prompt, and the method requires no additional training. PPAE uses the diffusion model’s cross-attention maps to support accurate local editing. It also combines local and global processing in a hierarchical pipeline, with the aim of making the overall editing process smoother.

These components address two connected needs: directing the change toward the relevant audio event and coordinating that local modification with the broader track. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness across various editing tasks. The contribution is a training-free editing mechanism that builds on information already available within diffusion models, extending their use from generating audio to controlling changes within existing audio.
icml-2024-prompt-guided-precise-audio-ed.tldr: PPAE uses diffusion cross-attention and a local-global pipeline for training-free audio editing guided by text prompts.

paragraphs: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model by training only a fraction of its parameters. This paper asks how far that idea can be simplified while reducing the trainable parameter count further. Its method uses random masking to select the parameters that are updated during fine-tuning.

The main empirical finding depends on an important training choice: a larger-than-expected learning rate. With that adjustment, random masking can match standard methods such as LoRA on various tasks while training fewer parameters. The result suggests that effective adaptation can emerge from a very simple parameter-selection mechanism when the optimization settings suit it.

The authors investigate this behavior both theoretically and empirically. They find that masking creates a flatter loss landscape and solutions farther away, which allows and necessitates large learning rates in their analysis. This explanation links the method’s effectiveness to how updates move through the optimization landscape. The contribution combines a simplified fine-tuning method with an account of why unusually large updates are central to its success.
icml-2024-random-masking-finds-winning-t.tldr: Random masking can match standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning with fewer trainable parameters when paired with sufficiently large learning rates.

paragraphs: Inverse constrained reinforcement learning infers behavioral constraints from expert demonstrations. Those constraints help a learner imitate expert preferences in safety-critical decisions. This paper shows that differences between training and deployment dynamics can undermine the inferred constraints and lead to unsafe movement, making environmental mismatch part of the learning problem.

The authors formulate Robust Constraint Inference and propose Adaptively Robust ICRL to solve it efficiently. They represent the effects of misspecified dynamics through an opponent policy, turning robust policy learning into a Markov game. The constraint model is then adjusted so that the learned policies align with expert demonstrations.

The behavioral modeling accommodates both soft and hard notions of optimality, allowing the constraint-learning procedure to work with these different descriptions of expert behavior. Experiments in continuous and discrete domains demonstrate the importance of robust constraints and the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. The contribution is an approach that explicitly incorporates dynamics mismatch into constraint inference, with empirical support for its usefulness in the tested environments.
icml-2024-robust-inverse-constrained-rei.tldr: AR-ICRL learns constraints from demonstrations while explicitly modeling dynamics mismatch through an adversarial Markov-game formulation.

paragraphs: Universal adversarial perturbations are small, image-independent modifications that can cause a neural network to misclassify many inputs. Their effectiveness may decline when the perturbation is transformed before being added to an image. This paper studies how to preserve attack effectiveness through changes such as scaling or altered pixel intensity.

The authors formulate transformation-robust universal perturbations and develop an iterative algorithm using probabilistic robustness bounds. The construction handles transformations formed by composing arbitrary sub-differentiable transformation functions. That condition defines the transformation family addressed by the method, while the probabilistic formulation captures robustness without treating every attack outcome as certain.

Evaluations on CIFAR-10 and ILSVRC 2012 examine transformations including rotation and contrast changes. Perturbations learned using primitive transformations also generalize well to tested unseen transformations, including fog and JPEG compression. The authors report up to 23% greater robustness than state-of-the-art baselines. The results show that transformation-aware construction can make a shared perturbation more persistent under the evaluated changes.
icml-2024-robust-universal-adversarial-p.tldr: An iterative method constructs universal adversarial perturbations that retain more attack effectiveness under tested real-world transformations.

paragraphs: Spectral graph neural networks process graph information through frequency-based representations. The paper identifies two common restrictions: filters are often limited to polynomial forms, and models are often designed for transductive use on relatively small graphs. SLOG addresses filter flexibility and applicability to large-scale inductive learning together.

For filtering, SLOG introduces a real-valued function with geometric interpretation, mathematical feasibility, and adaptive behavior beyond polynomial filters. For inductive learning, it combines subgraph sampling associated with spatial graph networks and signal-processing techniques from spectral networks. This connects spectral processing to a sampling approach suited to learning beyond a single fixed small graph.

Experiments on 16 datasets show superior results in inductive node classification for both homophilic and heterophilic graphs, where connected nodes tend to be similar or dissimilar, respectively. The findings support the combination of more flexible spectral filters and scalable sampling. The contribution is an architecture that broadens how spectral methods can be used while demonstrating benefits across both tested types of graph structure.
icml-2024-slog-an-inductive-spectral-gra.tldr: SLOG combines non-polynomial spectral filtering with subgraph sampling for inductive classification on large graphs.

paragraphs: Compressing a language model reduces its memory footprint but can also damage performance. This paper investigates a simple recovery technique: ordinary soft prompt tuning. The authors find that learned soft prompts can restore performance in compressed models without requiring a specially designed recovery mechanism for each compression framework.

A notable observation is that the recovery effect can transfer across tasks and models. This challenges the assumption that learned soft prompts must be tied to a single task. The transfer remains subject to tokenizer and dimensionality compatibility, so the finding does not imply that any prompt can be applied unchanged to any model.

The approach is compatible with pruning and quantization. On popular benchmarks, the authors demonstrate models compressed by up to eight times matching uncompressed counterparts, using joint four-bit quantization and 50% weight pruning. These results identify standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning as a potential tool for compression recovery. Transferable prompts could further reduce adaptation overhead by reusing recovery effects across compatible settings.
icml-2024-soft-prompt-recovers-compresse.tldr: Standard soft prompt tuning can recover compressed language-model performance, with transfer across compatible tasks and models.
